study_identification.title: Dissimilarity in Sulcal Width Patterns in the Cortex can be Used to Identify Patients With Schizophrenia With Extreme Deficits in Cognitive Performance

study_characteristics.study_objective: To determine whether lifespan PBSI-SW (person-based similarity index for sulcal width) trajectories differ between patients with schizophrenia and healthy subjects, whether differences are driven by individuals with extremely deviating PBSI-SW, and whether extreme PBSI-SW deviance is associated with deficits in cognition and sulcation index using a normative modeling approach.

dataset_name.answer: Utrecht Schizophrenia project; GROUP consortium (Genetic Risk and Outcome of Psychosis)

hc_age.answer: mean 31.04; sd 11.65 (baseline); mean 35.05; sd 11.88 (follow-up); range 16-70 years

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v5.1; BrainVISA v4.5 with Morphologist Toolbox

quality_checking_detail.answer: Combination of visual inspection and quantitative QA metrics (SNR, CNR, FBER, percent artifact voxels, Entropy); threshold for outliers defined as mean±2.698*SD for each metric; manual inspection performed in BrainVISA for sulcal labeling quality; 138 scans excluded based on quantitative QA metrics; 14 scans excluded after manual inspection; total 152 scans excluded from initial 1824 scans

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Scanner included as covariate in GAMM models. Two scanners used (Philips Intera or Achieva 1.5T, same vendor, field strength and acquisition protocol). All participants had baseline and follow-up scans on the same scanner.

modeling_method.answer: GAMLSS; Normative reference based on healthy controls

response_variable.answer: PBSI-SW (Person-Based Similarity Index for Sulcal Width); calculated from 11 bilateral sulcal regions

predictor_effects.answer: Age modeled with smooth function (spline); Scanner and total brain volume as fixed effects; Participant identifier as random effect

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly controlled for multiple nuisance variables in their normative modeling approach. Scanner effects were included as covariates in GAMM models. Total brain volume was included as a covariate. Age was modeled with smooth functions (splines) to account for nonlinearity. The PBSI-SW values were residualized for age, scanner, and total brain volume before creating normative references. The study also assessed image quality metrics systematically and excluded poor quality scans.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: GAMM models were implemented to examine age, diagnosis (ie, patient vs control), and an age × diagnosis interaction while controlling for scanner, total brain volume, and the random effect of the individual... PBSI-SW values were residualized for age, scanner, and total brain volume at each time point... we rigorously assessed the quality of the data using a combination of visual inspection and the examination of several quantitative quality assessments (QA) metrics
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text p.3 Methods section; Supplement p.5-6

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study used longitudinal data from the same cohort at two time points (baseline and follow-up). The normative reference was created from healthy controls, and the same healthy control group was assessed for fit. PBSI-SW-Z scores were calculated for both controls and patients at baseline and follow-up, with 10 controls identified as outliers (PBSI-SW-Z < -2), demonstrating validation on the training data.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not use an independent held-out test set from the same domain for validation. All healthy controls in the study were used to create the normative reference, and there was no mention of splitting the control group into training and test sets or using external independent healthy control data from the same datasets.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not validate the normative model using data from different domains or external datasets. All analyses were conducted within the Utrecht Schizophrenia project and GROUP consortium datasets. There was no mention of external validation on independent cohorts from different sites or studies.

clinical_groups_age.answer: mean 29.52; sd 8.95 (baseline); mean 33.60; sd 9.21 (follow-up); range 16-70 years at baseline

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (PBSI-SW-Z); threshold |PBSI-SW-Z| > 2 to identify outliers with markedly dissimilar morphometric profiles

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Generalized additive mixed models (GAMM) for age × diagnosis interaction; Welch t-tests for cross-sectional group comparisons at baseline and follow-up with PBSI-SW residualized for age, scanner, and total brain volume; Welch t-tests comparing outlier vs non-outlier patients on estimated IQ at baseline, PANSS scores, illness duration, and sulcation index; Nonparametric permutation testing (1000 permutations) for IQ comparison to address unbalanced sample sizes
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: A small subgroup of schizophrenia patients (19/164, 11.6%) with markedly deviant PBSI-SW (Z<-2) showed significantly lower estimated IQ at baseline (mean 89.00 vs 98.66, Cohen's d=-0.62, p<0.01) and lower sulcation index at follow-up (mean 1.60 vs 1.65, Cohen's d=-0.76, p=0.03) compared to non-outlier patients, and progressive reduction of PBSI-SW was driven by these deviating individuals.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The PBSI-SW trajectories showed significant age × diagnosis interaction (F=14.57, p<0.001), with patients displaying close to linear reduction with age while controls showed increase until age 30 then stability. Cross-sectional comparison at follow-up showed significant difference with small-to-intermediate effect size (mean difference=0.02, Cohen's d=0.36, p=0.001). Importantly, 19 patients (11.6%) had PBSI-SW-Z<-2 at any time point (vs 10 controls, χ²=3.06, p=0.04). Of these 19 outlier patients, 16 (84%) showed decrease in PBSI-SW-Z between baseline and follow-up (χ²=8.89, p<0.01), which is disproportionally high. When outliers were removed, the age × diagnosis interaction was no longer significant. Outlier patients had significantly lower estimated IQ at baseline (89.00±2.14 vs 98.66±1.64, t=-3.32, p<0.01, Cohen's d=-0.62), confirmed by nonparametric permutation testing (F=4.145, p<0.05). Outlier patients also showed lower sulcation index at follow-up compared to non-outlier patients (1.60±0.02 vs 1.65±0.01, t=-2.40, p=0.03, Cohen's d=-0.76). Patients overall had lower sulcation index than controls at follow-up (1.64±0.01 vs 1.68±0.01, Cohen's d=-0.38, p<0.01). PBSI-SW as continuous measure did not correlate with estimated IQ or sulcation index in the whole patient group. For comparison, PBSI-CT (cortical thickness) showed no progression over time and outliers did not differ in estimated IQ from non-outliers, suggesting increased sensitivity of sulcal width measures.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Small sample size of the outlier subgroup (19 patients, of which only 13 had IQ data available) limits statistical power for clinical characterization. Although no differences in image quality metrics were found between outliers and non-outliers, subtle effects of illness severity (e.g., increased motion during scanning) cannot be ruled out. Estimated IQ based on 4 WAIS subtests may have limitations compared to full-scale IQ scores, though it has shown good validity for general cognitive ability. Lack of information about development or premorbid adjustment. Age range could be extended to include adolescent-onset or childhood-onset schizophrenia. Need for validation in larger multicenter samples. No assessment of whether PBSI-SW deviance predicts treatment response or long-term outcomes.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This study demonstrates the utility of normative modeling for identifying biologically homogeneous subgroups in schizophrenia by leveraging interindividual heterogeneity rather than focusing on group averages. The PBSI-SW approach combines concepts of morphometric similarity and interindividual heterogeneity into a single multivariate summary measure. The finding that only 11.6% of patients showed marked deviance challenges the 'average patient' notion from traditional case-control designs. Sulcal width parameters appear more sensitive than cortical thickness to schizophrenia-associated atrophic changes over time. The association between PBSI-SW deviance, cognitive deficits, and reduced sulcation index (a marker of perinatal neurodevelopmental perturbations) supports the neurodevelopmental hypothesis of schizophrenia. Future applications could identify larger groups with marked deviance in multicenter samples for further clinical, cognitive, and biological characterization. The methodology is suitable for subtyping clinical populations based on neuroimaging-driven approaches.

general_notes.general_notes: This is one of the first studies to apply normative modeling to a multivariate morphometric similarity index (PBSI) rather than univariate measures. The study used sulcal width (SW) as the primary morphometric feature across 11 bilateral sulcal regions (22 ROIs total) based on BrainVISA segmentation. The 11 regions were: Calcarine, Frontal Medial, Parietal Occipital Medial, Sylvian Fissure, Occipital, Parietal, Prefrontal lateral, Central Sulcus, Precentral, Temporal basal, and Temporal lateral. These regions were selected based on previous studies showing sulcal morphological atypicalities in psychosis. PBSI-SW was calculated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficients between an individual's SW profile and the profiles of (other) controls. For patients, PBSI-SW was calculated as the average of correlations with all Nc controls. For controls, it was the average of correlations with other Nc-1 controls. Higher PBSI-SW (max=1) denotes greater similarity. The normative modeling approach extended the original PBSI method to index the degree of similarity between a patient's morphological profile and healthy controls. Z-scores were calculated using residualized PBSI-SW values after controlling for age, scanner, and total brain volume. The threshold of |Z|>2 is commonly used in normative modeling studies. Total of 656 scans from 328 participants (164 patients + 164 controls, each with 2 time points). Scan interval: mean 4.08 years (baseline to follow-up). Scanner distribution at baseline: Scanner I: 81 patients/55 controls; Scanner II: 83 patients/109 controls. Both scanners were Philips 1.5T with identical protocols. Mean age difference between groups at baseline was not significant when considering the full age range (16-70 years), though patients were slightly younger on average. Medication data available for only 82 patients at baseline and follow-up. No significant correlation between PBSI-SW and chlorpromazine equivalents or PANSS change scores (uncorrected correlation of 0.22 between baseline PBSI-SW and change in PANSS positive symptoms did not survive Bonferroni correction). The study also calculated symmetrized annual percent change (APC) for PBSI-SW and found 3 subjects with |Z|>5 for APC, but these did not show extreme values on quality metrics. Regional contribution analysis using leave-one-region-out method showed frontal regions contributed negatively to PBSI-SW in all groups, with only temporal basal region showing significant difference (higher contribution in non-outlier patients vs controls at follow-up after FDR correction, Cohen's d=-0.45). The study compared PBSI-SW results with those from Nispat software and found high correlation (r=0.94). Variability of PBSI-SW across lifespan was constant with no significant effects of age or diagnosis. R script for PBSI-SW calculation is available on GitHub. The study emphasizes the importance of focusing on interindividual differences in severity rather than just mean differences, consistent with Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework and recent biotype approaches to psychiatric classification.
